PART 1. PRELIMINARY
1.1 Introduction
Stress testing is a quantitative technique to measure the impact on a financial institution or
system in the event of exceptional but plausible incidents. Macro stress testing, as a methodology
of macroprudential analysis for assessing system risk as part of a financial stability supervisory
role, is widely used to evaluate financial stability in the event of exogenous shocks.
Since the global financial crisis (GFC), stress testing has become a well-established regulatory
tool to assess the resilience of the financial sector (Baudino, et al., 2018). Stress tests offer
quantitative, forward-looking evaluations of the financial system’s health and solvency under
various plausible scenarios. These tests can be designed with either a micro-prudential or
macroprudential policy focus. Macro stress tests, in particular, assess the financial system's
resilience using an adverse macroeconomic scenario that incorporates multiple risk factors. This
contrasts with sensitivity analysis, which examines the impact of specific risk factors in isolation,
without considering their interactions within the broader financial system.
Next to the prime responsibility of monetary policy, the responsibility to safeguard financial
stability features prominently in the mandate of the RMA. Therefore, DFRS has developed a
macro stress testing framework that will be used regularly for forward-looking financial
institution solvency assessments. Moreover, the importance of stress within the RMA is
reinforced by Risk Based Supervision, which requires tools to identify vulnerable financial
institutions both at a bank or non-bank level (micro-prudential) and a system-wide
(macro-prudential) perspective.
1.2 Objectives
The macro stress testing framework will be a policy toolkit to assess the resilience of Bhutan’s
financial system to adverse economic shocks by identifying systemic risks, evaluating their
potential impact, and supporting macro-prudential policy decisions. It helps strengthen financial
stability by integrating macro-financial linkages, enhancing data-driven risk assessment, and
ensuring effective regulatory oversight.

1.3 Scope
This stress testing framework is expected to be used for both top-down stress testing by
supervisors and bottom-up stress testing by financial institutions. These stress tests shall be
conducted under different macroeconomic scenarios designed by the supervisor. The top-down
stress testing conducted by the supervisor will project the stress test results using a set of
supervisory models that take as inputs bank-provided data on financial condition and risk
characteristics, as well as the supervisory scenarios. The stress test uses models developed or
selected by the supervisor, which may be refined each year in advance of the stress test. The
framework assesses various risk dimensions, including credit, market, liquidity, and operational
risks. Macro stress testing will be conducted over different time horizons, covering short-term
(six months to one year) and medium-term (one to three years) projections. The stress testing
will be conducted annually or depends on regulatory requirements.
1.4 Commencement
This framework shall:
(a) Be called “A Macro Stress Testing Framework for Solvency Assessment, 2025”;
(b) Come into force from 1st July 2025;
1.5 Score of Application
Apply to all the Financial Service Providers licensed/registered as per the FSA 2011.

PART 2. METHODOLOGY: FRAMEWORK
The proposed stress testing framework will use a structured, modular approach to assess the
resilience of financial institutions under adverse macroeconomic conditions. This framework is
adapted from the European Central Bank’s (ECB) solvency analysis, consisting of four
interrelated analytical pillars as shown in the figure below.
The first pillar (scenario design) entails creating macro-financial scenarios that will be applied to
the financial sector. These
scenarios include baseline and
adverse conditions, and take into
account key economic variables
such as GDP growth, inflation,
interest rates, and exchange rate
variations. The purpose is to
model probable financial stress
and assess how banks might
behave in various economic scenarios. The second pillar (top-down satellite models) consists of
models that translate macroeconomic scenarios into financial variables that directly affect
financial institutions' balance sheets. The third pillar (balance sheet) integrates the projected
models into individual financial institution balance sheets. This step allows for the calculation of
the impact on the solvency position of the financial institution, including capital adequacy and
risk-weighted asset changes. Finally, the fourth pillar (feedback) extends the analysis beyond the
initial impact on capital to assess second round effects. This includes evaluating the potential
contagion risk with the financial system and broader feedback loops to the real economy, such as
changes in credit supply and economic activity.

2.1 Macro-Financial Scenario Design
The objective of stress testing is to analyse the impact of potential shocks to the economy and
financial institutions. Based on one or more of the risk factors identified in the Financial
Stability reports, the scenarios will vary over time. In financial system oversight, risk factors
that are highly improbable but have serious repercussions for the economy and the financial
sector can easily be overlooked. Stress scenarios, therefore, apply shocks that would have
severe adverse consequences if they were to occur. The depth of scenarios, i.e., how severe
they are, will vary as a consequence of changes in the risk factors. At the same time,
projections for the baseline scenario and the uncertainty surrounding these projections will
have an impact on stress scenarios. In a downturn where economic developments are highly
uncertain and where risk factors can have serious consequences, the impact shown in the
stress test may be considerable.
(a) Macroeconomic Block
(i) The general starting point for any stress testing exercise, be it top-down or
bottom-up, is a set of macro-financial risks that could have a bearing on the
resilience of the banking system. Under this framework, the identification and
monitoring of systemic risks will be derived from its financial stability
surveillance exercises. The approach of mapping risks to scenarios should be
characterized by following important elements:
(ii) The scenarios should reflect severe but plausible outcomes, ensuring a level of
severity that significantly impacts banks while remaining realistic. This is
typically defined in probabilistic terms, considering both initial shocks (e.g.,
ROA or ROI changes) and their effects on key macroeconomic variables (e.g.,
GDP growth).
(iii) Macroeconomic scenarios for unemployment, GDP growth, land and building
valuation, inflation and monetary policy are generated exogenously using the
macro models. These scenarios are input as conditional assumption paths into a
reduced form of conditional satellite models to forecast credit risk, market risk
and profit model.
Page | 4

(iv) These scenarios should interact with the satellite models at the financial
institution level block, influencing the balance sheet and profit and loss accounts
across individual financial institutions. This process should generate paths for
Tier 1 capital resulting from the realization of the input macroeconomic
scenarios for the first year of the model run.
(v) The derived path for Tier 1 from the financial institution level block should be
used to calibrate a capital deleveraging shock in a structural Vector
Autoregression (SVAR) model (Refer Appendix A).
Figure 2 Scenario generation process
2.2 Financial Institution Level Block
The financial institution level block consists of two modules, Satellite models and Balance sheet.
The Satellite models comprises three main models: credit risk model, profit model and market
risk model. Beside three main models, the liquidity stress indicators should constitute an inherent
part of the solvency stress testing framework (Macro stress testing framework). These liquidity
stress indicators should be used from the liquidity stress testing framework, in the form of market
liquidity (the risk that an asset can not be sold or used as collateral) or funding liquidity (the risk
that financial institutions are unable to roll-over maturity funding).
Page | 5

The credit risk model and profit model should impact the profit and loss account through
impairments and net interest income, respectively, and ultimately capital through retained
earnings in the capital account. The credit risk models should use the credit parameters such as
probability of default (PD), Loss Given Default (LGD) and Exposure at Default to obtain the
estimate for expected credit losses over the scenario horizon. The assumptions and projections
from the satellite modules are translated into revenues, expenses, losses and provisions. Further,
the profit model should translate projections on interest rates and assumptions on balance sheet
growth into interest income and expense. The approach can be divided into four modules: the net
interest income calculation, the loan losses and impairment calculation, the market risk
calculation and the final profit and loss calculation. Under the balance sheet module, it should
calculate interest income and interest expenses dependent on the macro scenario projections.
Figure 3 Profit and Loss Calculation Process
At the macro level, financial institution level capital depletion will be aggregated to estimate the
impact on the system-wide capital position for a given macroeconomic projection. The solvency
calculation should comprise of the definition and calculation method of capital, which includes
net income and Total Risk Weighted Assets (RWA). Therefore, solvency ratio is calculated as the
sum of the existing capital stock and earnings accumulated over the stress period in relation to
Page | 6

the end-horizon risk-weighted assets, as shown in figure 4. The composition of capital should be
aligned with the standard definition set by the regulator.
Figure 4 Solvency Calculation Process
2.3 Feedback Analysis
Macro stress test exercises typically end once the first-round impact on the stressed financial
institutions’ solvency position is derived. However, in reality it is to be expected that banks
would react to stressed situations by adjusting their balance sheets in certain ways, which in turn
could have ramifications on the real economy and on other banks in the system. To analyse such
effects, financial network analysis tools should be applied. Such actions, for example in the form
of loan supply restrictions, could be expected to have real economic implications which would
tend to amplify the original adverse macroeconomic scenario. To account for such feedback
effects linking results from the stress testing framework to the broader economy requires
macroeconomic models with financial sector interfaces that can derive the macroeconomic
implications of shocks hitting the financial sector.

(a) Data and Estimation Approach
The model is recommended to use the following key shocks:
(i) Aggregate Demand Shocks ( e.g., Fluctuation in Balance of Trade, domestic
consumption, high unemployment rate)
(ii) Aggregate Supply Shock (e.g. hydropower disruptions, inflation spikes)
(iii) Monetary Policy Shock (e.g. Increase in CRR, central bank interest rate
adjustment)
(iv) Capital Deleveraging Shock (e.g. bank capital tightening due to rising NPLs)
